doc.title: John Lamb interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clearwater Beach, Florida, March 16, 2001

title: Mentor Dean Earl and choosing a school
summary: Bandleader Dean Earl teaches him manners, professionalism and sensible habits and steers him away from Berklee toward a teaching degree.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: School days: grades, teachers and leaving school

blocks.x: and he says, “good sound.” And you know, encouragement. And in this little joint, Eddie Levine’s, I met all kinds of musicians, they used to come up and visit our leader, who was Dean Earl. And as far as my style and being a gentleman and being in the business and all that, was a fellow by the name of, like I said, his name was Dean Earl. And he talked about good manners and musicianship and personality, being on and off the stand, and not drinking excessively. He says, “if you’re going to drink, always have a good meal first.” You know, that type of thing. And so he was like a mentor. And so Dean was also a graduate of Berklee. He also taught there and all those things. And he advised me as far as schools are concerned. He says, “if I were you,” he says, “I would go to a different school.” He says, “Berklee doesn’t offer you a teaching degree.” So I thought about it, so I went over to the New England Conservatory and I hang around the practice room a little bit, just getting the feel of things and all that. And in the meantime at the Hi-Hat across the street, I used to hear all of these groups come in, all these small groups. Guys like Shadow Wilson and Miles Davis and Ella Fitzgerald and Hot Lips Page, and all those kind of people. And then there was another place called The Shell Bone, not The Shell Bone, there was a famous club in New Orleans at one time, there was another club in Boston, George Wein—
